steps.title: Why does the countdown keep going?
steps.objective: Diagnose the source's inline countdown quiz without running an unbounded loop.
steps.explanation:
Syntax errors violate language grammar; semantic errors violate your intended behavior, often while compiling successfully. They can cause wrong results, erratic behavior, data corruption, crashes, or no visible symptom on tested inputs. Warnings and testing help, but neither proves correctness.

The source's inline quiz intends to count five through one, announce launch at zero, then stop. Unsigned decrement at zero wraps to the type's maximum: defined arithmetic, but the wrong algorithm. Reason about this unbounded listing without running it or assuming an unsigned width.

Adapted from [LearnCpp 9.3, Infinite loops](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/), Alex; published December 21, 2020, updated November 10, 2024. This is the page's inline diagnosis quiz; it has no formal end quiz or coding assignment.
steps.sourceExercise: adapted source inline quiz — Infinite loops: diagnose the unsigned countdown that should print five through one and a launch message, then stop

questions.question: After the first launch message, why does the loop continue?
options: Unsigned decrement at zero must crash.
The counter wraps to its maximum value, and every unsigned value satisfies >= 0.
The loop condition is checked only once.
Zero is not representable by unsigned int.
questions.explanation: The comparison never becomes false. Wraparound is defined for unsigned arithmetic, but defeats this termination design. The maximum value depends on the type's width.

steps.title: Make progress and include the endpoint
steps.objective: Implement two finite loops with correct first, last, and zero cases.
steps.explanation:
Trace entry, progress, and endpoint. For strictly above four, `x >= 4` wrongly admits equality. With n == 4, `for (int i{1}; i > n; ++i)` never enters; `i < n` misses the endpoint; forgetting `++i` can repeat forever. Test the boundary itself, not just a typical interior value.

Implement both functions for 0 <= n <= 20: ascending(n) returns one through n, each followed by a space (empty at zero). countdown(n) returns n through one, each followed by a space, then Launch! with no trailing space (just Launch! at zero). Use a signed downward counter and stop at zero. The placeholder starter is finite.

New repair practice based on [LearnCpp 9.3, Conditional logic errors, Infinite loops, and Off-by-one errors](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/).

steps.title: Read the expression the compiler sees
steps.objective: Distinguish grouping, assignment, and function reference from the intended operations.
steps.explanation:
- Grouping: `!x > y` means `(!x) > y`, not `!(x > y)`. Likewise, `member || guest && open` groups guest with open; require `(member || guest) && open` when opening hours apply to everyone.
- Mutation: `if (permission = 'y')` assigns a nonzero character, then converts it to true; `==` compares without overwriting input. Investigate assignment warnings rather than hiding them with parentheses.
- Invocation: for a function returning 6, `readLevel()` produces 6; `readLevel` instead yields a function pointer here. Its explicit Boolean conversion is true (printed as 1 by default), and does not call the function. Direct streaming commonly also selects Boolean output.

New diagnosis question based on [LearnCpp 9.3, Incorrect operator precedence, Using assignment instead of equality, and Forgetting the function call operator](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/).

questions.question: Which review correctly fixes all three intentions: negate the whole comparison, compare permission, and obtain the function's result?
questions.explanation: Parentheses select the comparison to negate; == avoids mutation; () invokes the function instead of converting its address.

steps.title: Trace the types before trusting the number
steps.objective: Explain integer truncation and floating-point approximation as distinct sources of numeric error.
steps.explanation:
Two int operands perform integer division, discarding the fraction before assignment or a later cast. Convert an operand first: `static_cast<double>(7) / 2` retains the fraction; `static_cast<double>(7 / 2)` cannot recover it. Validate the divisor before calculating.

Floating-point storage is finite too: `float f{0.123456789f};` may lose digits on storage, and printing may round further. More output digits cannot restore lost information. On ordinary binary floating point, repeated additions of 0.1 can accumulate error, so an expected 1.0 may fail ==; != has the corresponding problem. Choose sufficient storage precision and an application-scaled tolerance for approximate comparisons, rather than replacing every equality mechanically.

New activity based on [LearnCpp 9.3, Precision issues with floating point types and Integer division](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/).
steps.sourceExercise: supplementary — combined numeric demonstrations, with portable division output and a floating-point reasoning question

questions.question: What is printed?
questions.explanation: The first expression converts the already-truncated quotient 3. The second converts total first, so the division retains the fraction.

questions.question: A measurement sums ten 0.1 terms. Which policy addresses possible rounding error when comparing the result with 1.0?
options: Print more digits, then require exact equality.
Use a tolerance chosen for the measurement's scale and acceptable error.
Replace == with != to eliminate the rounding error.
questions.explanation: Formatting does not change the stored approximation, and != only negates equality. A suitable tolerance reflects the measurement requirement.

steps.title: Keep both actions behind the permission check
steps.objective: Use one compound statement to control two related actions.
steps.explanation:
Without braces, if controls one statement regardless of indentation. In `if (allowed); launch();`, that statement is an empty semicolon, so launch runs unconditionally. In `if (allowed) prepare(); launch();`, only prepare is guarded. Also, `if (allowed) if (ready) launch(); else deny();` attaches else to the inner if; brace the outer body before else when denial belongs to the outer decision.

Repair launchMessage(char permission): only lowercase 'y' authorizes it. Return exactly `Preparing\nSimulated launch\n` when authorized, otherwise an empty string. Group both appends in the permission branch. The starter safely constructs a string; test rejected as well as accepted inputs.

New repair practice based on [LearnCpp 9.3, Accidental null statements and Not using a compound statement when one is required](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/), including its dangling-else warning.

steps.title: Repair the average-score calculation
steps.objective: Apply guards, floating-point division, and complete return paths in the existing workspace.
steps.explanation:
Open the [workspace notes](workspaces/09/09_03/lesson.md) and [source](workspaces/09/09_03/main.cpp). Implement averageScore(total, count), with inputs at most 10000: return -1.0 for total < 0 or count <= 0; otherwise return the floating-point quotient. Predict (5, 2) -> 2.5, (0, 3) -> 0.0, and (5, 0) -> -1.0 before running.

Reason first: what output is guaranteed if code divides integers by zero, reads an uninitialized automatic int, or falls off a double-returning function? None: those paths have undefined behavior in C++20. Guard before dividing, convert an operand first, initialize before reading, and return on every path. Keep the supplied tests, add (0, 0) -> -1.0, and explain why invalid count overrides valid zero total. Change one cause at a time and rerun earlier passing cases.

Run the existing workspace tests, then submit with `./course check 9.3`. This is the [repository assignment](lessons/09_03.json), supplementing [LearnCpp 9.3](https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/common-semantic-errors-in-c/), not a source-page coding task.
